case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old woman presented with painless vision reduction and eye redness in the right eye for a week. The initial best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 4/20 (approximately 20/100), and an irregular superficial corneal ulcer with an epithelial defect size of 3 mm × 5 mm was found in the center of edematous cornea. She received penetrating keratoplasty 4 months later, as the ulcer did not heal with intensive medication. Then, topical tobramycin dexamethasone, topical tacrolimus, and daily oral prednisone, 40 mg, were prescribed, with a gradual taper of prednisone to a maintenance dose of 10 mg. At 5-month postoperative follow-up, some thin snowflakelike matter was found deposited on the iris and in the angle, with rare cell and mild flare in the anterior chamber. She was then diagnosed with uveitis and subsequently prescribed topical prednisone, subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide, oral prednisone, 40 mg, and daily intravenous ganciclovir, 5 mg/kg. An aqueous sample was obtained for diagnostic polymerase chain reaction, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was detected with a DNA load of 3.12 × 107cells. Nine months after the keratoplasty, when she presented to the Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center, her BCVA was 2/100 OD (approximately 20/1000 OD), and her intraocular pressure was 19 mm Hg. Diffuse tiny nodules were observed all over the iris, along with more snowflake and severe cataract (Figure 1A). The fundus could not be seen. B-ultrasonography showed a dense opacity in the anterior vitreous body (Figure 1B).

case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. The most common type is monomorphic PTLD, including B-cell subtypes (more than 70%) and T-cell subtypes (less than 5%).5Less than 5% of PTLD is classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Even though PTLD usually involves lymphoid-rich organ or tissue, various cases of extranodal organ involvement have been reported.6Ocular involvement is uncommon and can be easily misdiagnosed for masquerade feature, such as iris nodule, subretinal mass, anterior chamber flare, or vitreous opacity.7,8 Algros et al9reported a case of gastric PTLD in a patient after keratoplasty who was diagnosed with EBV-induced gastric PTLD (B-cell lymphoma) after receiving oral cyclosporine for a year. Similarly, this patient had received systemic prednisone for 5 months, which might cause her immunosuppressive condition. Central nervous system lymphoma involvement was ruled out by enhanced 3.0-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. Systemic and topical prednisone along with topical tacrolimus were discontinued on diagnosis. Intravitreal methotrexate (methotrexate, 0.4 mg) was given every 2 weeks for a total of 5 doses.10As cataract progressed, extracapsular cataract extraction was performed without intraocular lens implantation, while its impact on PTLD was unclear. The anterior chamber deposit, iris nodules, and vitreous opacity had resolved. There were no obvious retinal lesions. EBV DNA load from aqueous humor was 0 at the fifth methotrexate injection, without antiviral medication. Unfortunately, she developed corneal edema, presumably associated with chronic endothelial dysfunction, which might be due to PTLD as well as repeated intraocular procedures. At 1-year follow-up, her BCVA was 1/100 OD (approximately counting fingers OD) and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg, without recurrent sign of iris nodules.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

   Scoring:

[Clinical case]
A 62-year-old woman presented with painless vision reduction and eye redness in the right eye for a week. The initial best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 4/20 (approximately 20/100), and an irregular superficial corneal ulcer with an epithelial defect size of 3 mm × 5 mm was found in the center of edematous cornea. She received penetrating keratoplasty 4 months later, as the ulcer did not heal with intensive medication. Then, topical tobramycin dexamethasone, topical tacrolimus, and daily oral prednisone, 40 mg, were prescribed, with a gradual taper of prednisone to a maintenance dose of 10 mg. At 5-month postoperative follow-up, some thin snowflakelike matter was found deposited on the iris and in the angle, with rare cell and mild flare in the anterior chamber. She was then diagnosed with uveitis and subsequently prescribed topical prednisone, subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide, oral prednisone, 40 mg, and daily intravenous ganciclovir, 5 mg/kg. An aqueous sample was obtained for diagnostic polymerase chain reaction, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was detected with a DNA load of 3.12 × 107cells. Nine months after the keratoplasty, when she presented to the Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center, her BCVA was 2/100 OD (approximately 20/1000 OD), and her intraocular pressure was 19 mm Hg. Diffuse tiny nodules were observed all over the iris, along with more snowflake and severe cataract (Figure 1A). The fundus could not be seen. B-ultrasonography showed a dense opacity in the anterior vitreous body (Figure 1B).

[Dialogue history so far]
[Doctor]: Given the presence of EBV detected in the aqueous sample and the worsening vision, the most appropriate next step in management is to perform an intravitreal injection of ganciclovir to target the viral infection directly and potentially improve her visual outcomes.
[AI Assistant]: I disagree with that recommendation. Intravitreal ganciclovir is typically considered for cytomegalovirus retinitis, but EBV-associated uveitis is a distinct entity that may not respond to direct intravitreal antiviral therapy; the systemic ganciclovir she is already receiving is the standard systemic antiviral for this situation. The worsening vision and dense vitreous opacities in this case are more likely due to severe inflammatory sequelae, so the priority should be to intensify anti-inflammatory management, possibly with systemic immunosuppression, rather than adding a local antiviral injection.

case_info.caption: A, The iris showed atrophy, along with severe cataract, a diffuse white tiny nodular on the iris (pink arrowhead), and a small pile of snowflakelike deposit (yellow arrowhead). B, A massive opacity at anterior vitreous body (blue arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. The most common type is monomorphic PTLD, including B-cell subtypes (more than 70%) and T-cell subtypes (less than 5%).5Less than 5% of PTLD is classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Even though PTLD usually involves lymphoid-rich organ or tissue, various cases of extranodal organ involvement have been reported.6Ocular involvement is uncommon and can be easily misdiagnosed for masquerade feature, such as iris nodule, subretinal mass, anterior chamber flare, or vitreous opacity.7,8 Algros et al9reported a case of gastric PTLD in a patient after keratoplasty who was diagnosed with EBV-induced gastric PTLD (B-cell lymphoma) after receiving oral cyclosporine for a year. Similarly, this patient had received systemic prednisone for 5 months, which might cause her immunosuppressive condition. Central nervous system lymphoma involvement was ruled out by enhanced 3.0-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. Systemic and topical prednisone along with topical tacrolimus were discontinued on diagnosis. Intravitreal methotrexate (methotrexate, 0.4 mg) was given every 2 weeks for a total of 5 doses.10As cataract progressed, extracapsular cataract extraction was performed without intraocular lens implantation, while its impact on PTLD was unclear. The anterior chamber deposit, iris nodules, and vitreous opacity had resolved. There were no obvious retinal lesions. EBV DNA load from aqueous humor was 0 at the fifth methotrexate injection, without antiviral medication. Unfortunately, she developed corneal edema, presumably associated with chronic endothelial dysfunction, which might be due to PTLD as well as repeated intraocular procedures. At 1-year follow-up, her BCVA was 1/100 OD (approximately counting fingers OD) and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg, without recurrent sign of iris nodules.

case_info.caption: A, The iris showed atrophy, along with severe cataract, a diffuse white tiny nodular on the iris (pink arrowhead), and a small pile of snowflakelike deposit (yellow arrowhead). B, A massive opacity at anterior vitreous body (blue arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. The most common type is monomorphic PTLD, including B-cell subtypes (more than 70%) and T-cell subtypes (less than 5%).5Less than 5% of PTLD is classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Even though PTLD usually involves lymphoid-rich organ or tissue, various cases of extranodal organ involvement have been reported.6Ocular involvement is uncommon and can be easily misdiagnosed for masquerade feature, such as iris nodule, subretinal mass, anterior chamber flare, or vitreous opacity.7,8 Algros et al9reported a case of gastric PTLD in a patient after keratoplasty who was diagnosed with EBV-induced gastric PTLD (B-cell lymphoma) after receiving oral cyclosporine for a year. Similarly, this patient had received systemic prednisone for 5 months, which might cause her immunosuppressive condition. Central nervous system lymphoma involvement was ruled out by enhanced 3.0-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. Systemic and topical prednisone along with topical tacrolimus were discontinued on diagnosis. Intravitreal methotrexate (methotrexate, 0.4 mg) was given every 2 weeks for a total of 5 doses.10As cataract progressed, extracapsular cataract extraction was performed without intraocular lens implantation, while its impact on PTLD was unclear. The anterior chamber deposit, iris nodules, and vitreous opacity had resolved. There were no obvious retinal lesions. EBV DNA load from aqueous humor was 0 at the fifth methotrexate injection, without antiviral medication. Unfortunately, she developed corneal edema, presumably associated with chronic endothelial dysfunction, which might be due to PTLD as well as repeated intraocular procedures. At 1-year follow-up, her BCVA was 1/100 OD (approximately counting fingers OD) and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg, without recurrent sign of iris nodules.

case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. The most common type is monomorphic PTLD, including B-cell subtypes (more than 70%) and T-cell subtypes (less than 5%).5Less than 5% of PTLD is classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Even though PTLD usually involves lymphoid-rich organ or tissue, various cases of extranodal organ involvement have been reported.6Ocular involvement is uncommon and can be easily misdiagnosed for masquerade feature, such as iris nodule, subretinal mass, anterior chamber flare, or vitreous opacity.7,8 Algros et al9reported a case of gastric PTLD in a patient after keratoplasty who was diagnosed with EBV-induced gastric PTLD (B-cell lymphoma) after receiving oral cyclosporine for a year. Similarly, this patient had received systemic prednisone for 5 months, which might cause her immunosuppressive condition. Central nervous system lymphoma involvement was ruled out by enhanced 3.0-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. Systemic and topical prednisone along with topical tacrolimus were discontinued on diagnosis. Intravitreal methotrexate (methotrexate, 0.4 mg) was given every 2 weeks for a total of 5 doses.10As cataract progressed, extracapsular cataract extraction was performed without intraocular lens implantation, while its impact on PTLD was unclear. The anterior chamber deposit, iris nodules, and vitreous opacity had resolved. There were no obvious retinal lesions. EBV DNA load from aqueous humor was 0 at the fifth methotrexate injection, without antiviral medication. Unfortunately, she developed corneal edema, presumably associated with chronic endothelial dysfunction, which might be due to PTLD as well as repeated intraocular procedures. At 1-year follow-up, her BCVA was 1/100 OD (approximately counting fingers OD) and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg, without recurrent sign of iris nodules.

case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. The most common type is monomorphic PTLD, including B-cell subtypes (more than 70%) and T-cell subtypes (less than 5%).5Less than 5% of PTLD is classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Even though PTLD usually involves lymphoid-rich organ or tissue, various cases of extranodal organ involvement have been reported.6Ocular involvement is uncommon and can be easily misdiagnosed for masquerade feature, such as iris nodule, subretinal mass, anterior chamber flare, or vitreous opacity.7,8 Algros et al9reported a case of gastric PTLD in a patient after keratoplasty who was diagnosed with EBV-induced gastric PTLD (B-cell lymphoma) after receiving oral cyclosporine for a year. Similarly, this patient had received systemic prednisone for 5 months, which might cause her immunosuppressive condition. Central nervous system lymphoma involvement was ruled out by enhanced 3.0-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. Systemic and topical prednisone along with topical tacrolimus were discontinued on diagnosis. Intravitreal methotrexate (methotrexate, 0.4 mg) was given every 2 weeks for a total of 5 doses.10As cataract progressed, extracapsular cataract extraction was performed without intraocular lens implantation, while its impact on PTLD was unclear. The anterior chamber deposit, iris nodules, and vitreous opacity had resolved. There were no obvious retinal lesions. EBV DNA load from aqueous humor was 0 at the fifth methotrexate injection, without antiviral medication. Unfortunately, she developed corneal edema, presumably associated with chronic endothelial dysfunction, which might be due to PTLD as well as repeated intraocular procedures. At 1-year follow-up, her BCVA was 1/100 OD (approximately counting fingers OD) and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg, without recurrent sign of iris nodules.

case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. The most common type is monomorphic PTLD, including B-cell subtypes (more than 70%) and T-cell subtypes (less than 5%).5Less than 5% of PTLD is classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Even though PTLD usually involves lymphoid-rich organ or tissue, various cases of extranodal organ involvement have been reported.6Ocular involvement is uncommon and can be easily misdiagnosed for masquerade feature, such as iris nodule, subretinal mass, anterior chamber flare, or vitreous opacity.7,8 Algros et al9reported a case of gastric PTLD in a patient after keratoplasty who was diagnosed with EBV-induced gastric PTLD (B-cell lymphoma) after receiving oral cyclosporine for a year. Similarly, this patient had received systemic prednisone for 5 months, which might cause her immunosuppressive condition. Central nervous system lymphoma involvement was ruled out by enhanced 3.0-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. Systemic and topical prednisone along with topical tacrolimus were discontinued on diagnosis. Intravitreal methotrexate (methotrexate, 0.4 mg) was given every 2 weeks for a total of 5 doses.10As cataract progressed, extracapsular cataract extraction was performed without intraocular lens implantation, while its impact on PTLD was unclear. The anterior chamber deposit, iris nodules, and vitreous opacity had resolved. There were no obvious retinal lesions. EBV DNA load from aqueous humor was 0 at the fifth methotrexate injection, without antiviral medication. Unfortunately, she developed corneal edema, presumably associated with chronic endothelial dysfunction, which might be due to PTLD as well as repeated intraocular procedures. At 1-year follow-up, her BCVA was 1/100 OD (approximately counting fingers OD) and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg, without recurrent sign of iris nodules.

case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old woman presented with painless vision reduction and eye redness in the right eye for a week. The initial best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 4/20 (approximately 20/100), and an irregular superficial corneal ulcer with an epithelial defect size of 3 mm × 5 mm was found in the center of edematous cornea. She received penetrating keratoplasty 4 months later, as the ulcer did not heal with intensive medication. Then, topical tobramycin dexamethasone, topical tacrolimus, and daily oral prednisone, 40 mg, were prescribed, with a gradual taper of prednisone to a maintenance dose of 10 mg. At 5-month postoperative follow-up, some thin snowflakelike matter was found deposited on the iris and in the angle, with rare cell and mild flare in the anterior chamber. She was then diagnosed with uveitis and subsequently prescribed topical prednisone, subconjunctival triamcinolone acetonide, oral prednisone, 40 mg, and daily intravenous ganciclovir, 5 mg/kg. An aqueous sample was obtained for diagnostic polymerase chain reaction, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was detected with a DNA load of 3.12 × 107cells. Nine months after the keratoplasty, when she presented to the Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center, her BCVA was 2/100 OD (approximately 20/1000 OD), and her intraocular pressure was 19 mm Hg. Diffuse tiny nodules were observed all over the iris, along with more snowflake and severe cataract (Figure 1A). The fundus could not be seen. B-ultrasonography showed a dense opacity in the anterior vitreous body (Figure 1B).

case_info.explanation: Ocular polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders in the left eye C. Repeat aqueous sampling with an iris biopsy Although EBV had been detected with high DNA load, intravitreal ganciclovir was not recommended (choice A), as there was no evidence-based antiviral drug for EBV.1Nonetheless, EBV-associated diseases, such as uveitis, viral endophthalmitis, or cellular proliferative disease, should be considered. Her iris nodules and atypical anterior chamber deposits were uncommon in uveitis or viral endophthalmitis, which supported our consideration of a cellular proliferative condition. Therefore, we thought repeated aqueous sampling without an iris biopsy could not assess the pathological nature of the nodules directly (choice B); we also chose to withhold intravitreal corticosteroids (choice D) until results of the iris biopsy were known. The iris specimen was composed of a polymorphic mixture of lymphoid cells that include medium-sized to enlarged irregular lymphocytes. The tumor cells showed nuclear atypia and expressed B-cell antigens (diffuse positivity for CD20 and CD79a) and were EBV positive by Epstein-Barr encoding region in situ hybridization (Figure 2). Genetic studies showed gene rearrangement of immunoglobulin heavy chain, immunoglobulin κ light chain, and immunoglobulin light chain loci. A diagnosis of polymorphic posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorders (PTLD) associated with EBV infection was made by a lymphoma subspecialty pathologist. PTLD is defined as a series of complications that occur after organ transplant or hematopoietic cell transplant, characterized by varying degrees of lymphocyte hyperplasia, ranging from benign hyperplasia to malignant lymphomas.2PTLD usually arise under immunosuppressive condition and are mainly (around 85%) driven by EBV.2,3PTLD can be divided into 4 histological categories.4Early lesions and polymorphic PTLD account for about 5% and 15% to 20% of PTLD, respectively. The most common type is monomorphic PTLD, including B-cell subtypes (more than 70%) and T-cell subtypes (less than 5%).5Less than 5% of PTLD is classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Even though PTLD usually involves lymphoid-rich organ or tissue, various cases of extranodal organ involvement have been reported.6Ocular involvement is uncommon and can be easily misdiagnosed for masquerade feature, such as iris nodule, subretinal mass, anterior chamber flare, or vitreous opacity.7,8 Algros et al9reported a case of gastric PTLD in a patient after keratoplasty who was diagnosed with EBV-induced gastric PTLD (B-cell lymphoma) after receiving oral cyclosporine for a year. Similarly, this patient had received systemic prednisone for 5 months, which might cause her immunosuppressive condition. Central nervous system lymphoma involvement was ruled out by enhanced 3.0-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. Systemic and topical prednisone along with topical tacrolimus were discontinued on diagnosis. Intravitreal methotrexate (methotrexate, 0.4 mg) was given every 2 weeks for a total of 5 doses.10As cataract progressed, extracapsular cataract extraction was performed without intraocular lens implantation, while its impact on PTLD was unclear. The anterior chamber deposit, iris nodules, and vitreous opacity had resolved. There were no obvious retinal lesions. EBV DNA load from aqueous humor was 0 at the fifth methotrexate injection, without antiviral medication. Unfortunately, she developed corneal edema, presumably associated with chronic endothelial dysfunction, which might be due to PTLD as well as repeated intraocular procedures. At 1-year follow-up, her BCVA was 1/100 OD (approximately counting fingers OD) and intraocular pressure was 12 mm Hg, without recurrent sign of iris nodules.
